You are on your knees in the mud at Agincourt, and the weight on your back will not let you rise. Your armour has worked. No sword has opened you. No arrow has found its gap. And you are going to die anyway — face-down, with no wound at all.

That is the knight Hollywood almost never shows you. The movies give him polished steel, a clear patch of ground and one worthy opponent. niche.title: How Did Surgeons Operate Before Anesthesia?
niche.description:
How Did Surgeons Operate Before Anesthesia?

A leather strap between your teeth, strong men holding you down, a box of sawdust under the table, and a surgeon racing the clock. For thousands of years, this was surgery. In this video we follow how surgeons operated without anesthesia, from opium sponges and boiling oil to Frances Burney's harrowing letter, the laughing gas shows, the Ether Dome in Boston and the myth of Robert Liston's "300 percent" operation. Vacuum-assisted wound therapy used a sealed dressing and gentle suction to remove fluid and protect damaged tissue. The method came from the work of Louis Argenta and Michael Morykwas before military hospitals applied it to severe blast wounds. niche.title: Les Petites Curies: Marie Curie's X-Ray Vans (1914)
niche.description:
September 1914. German troops are closing in on Paris, and Madame Marie Curie boards a government train to Bordeaux with one gram of radium – France's entire research supply – to keep it safe from the war.

Back in Paris she sees the real problem: surgeons at the front can't find the bullets and shrapnel inside the wounded. So she talks wealthy friends out of their cars, has them turned into mobile X-ray vans, learns to drive and takes her 17-year-old daughter Irène along as her assistant. The soldiers have a nickname for the vans: "les petites Curies" – the little Curies.

niche.title: Brutal Surgery That Kept Rome Alive
niche.description:

When young legionary Marcus is struck by a barbed arrow during an enemy horse archer ambush, survival comes down to the Roman army's frontline combat medics: the Capsari and field surgeons like Lucius. From field tourniquets to extraction spoons, honey dressings, and red-hot iron cauterization, discover the brutal realities of ancient military medicine that kept legions standing.

In 1868, this physician used Dutch medical training while armies fought across Japan. He faced gunshot wounds, weak transport, and a country divided by war. His work shows how one doctor helped connect older Japanese healing with modern surgery and medical training. The change began with wounded men who needed help immediately. Five simple words recorded in a Civil War field hospital. But behind them stood a surgeon whose service extended across some of the war’s bloodiest campaigns.

Surgeon George W. Metcalf of the 76th New York began his military medical career in 1861. From South Mountain to Gettysburg, he treated wounded soldiers, monitored the condition of his regiment, and performed battlefield surgery.

At Gettysburg in July 1863, he performed a documented shoulder amputation on a wounded soldier of his own regiment.

Months later, Metcalf recorded Private D. Rapp’s wound at th

niche.title: How Did Civil War Surgeons Save More Limbs? #Shorts
niche.description: At Gettysburg, a shattered leg could leave a surgeon with an awful choice: remove the limb quickly or try to save it. Both paths could kill the wounded soldier. In July 1863, doctors such as Daniel M. S. B. Smith recorded what happened inside crowded field hospitals. They studied broken bones, deep wounds, infection, and the narrow line between repair and amputation. Those records helped military surgeons learn which limbs could be saved and which operations gave a soldier the best chance to live. The battlefield became a harsh laboratory for future bone surgery. If you enjoy Gettysburg histor

niche.title: Why Did Harold Gillies Rebuild Faces in WWI? #Shorts
niche.description: A soldier could live through a battlefield wound and still lose the face his family knew. During World War I, Harold Gillies tried to change that at Queen Mary's Hospital in Sidcup. The video follows how surgeons handled shattered jaws, missing skin, and wounds that needed many operations. Gillies used skin grafts, dental plates, and careful drawings because no modern facial surgery guide existed yet. His patients faced pain, long hospital stays, and the hard task of seeing themselves again. If you enjoy human stories from military and medical history, this story is for you.

niche.title: Where does "bite the bullet" come from? (It's not battlefield surgery)
niche.description:

So where does bite the bullet come from? Everyone tells the surgery story. Nope. I went digging, and the evidence for that one is honestly pretty flimsy, while the real trail runs through 1700s soldiers who had to stay quiet and a Rudyard Kipling novel from 1891.

Next time you have to bite the bullet, you'll know why.
